summary: God’s eternal, sovereign, gracious choice; election in Christ before the foundation of the world
readingInstruction: Read Ephesians 1:3-14 and Romans 9:1-24. Today is a doctrinal pause on election and predestination. Read slowly and with humility. Notice the repeated phrase “in him” in Ephesians and the emphasis on God’s mercy in Romans.
settingTheScene: Few doctrines have been as debated as election, and few are as comforting when understood. The word means choosing. Ephesians 1 speaks of God choosing us in Christ before the foundation of the world. Romans 9 stresses that God’s purpose of election works by his mercy, not by human merit or descent. The doctrine is not meant to start arguments but to produce worship, humility, and security. Notice that Ephesians 1 is written in a hymn of praise.
observation: “Even as he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and blameless before him” (Ephesians 1:4).
“He predestined us for adoption as sons through Jesus Christ, according to the purpose of his will” (Ephesians 1:5).
“To the praise of his glorious grace, with which he has blessed us in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6).
“In him we have obtained an inheritance, having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will” (Ephesians 1:11).
“In order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls” (Romans 9:11).
“For he says to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion” (Romans 9:15).
“So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy” (Romans 9:16).
“In order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, which he has prepared beforehand for glory” (Romans 9:23).
doctrinalFocus:
Election is God’s choice, before creation and from his own mercy, of a people to be saved in Christ. Predestination is closely related and speaks of God determining beforehand the destiny of those he has chosen: adoption, holiness, and glory. The Bible uses these words, so Christians must take them seriously. They are not ideas of a particular school but of Scripture.

The central point is clear in every tradition: salvation is God’s gift, not human achievement. The Father chose us “in him,” in Christ. We are not chosen because of foreseen goodness. We were chosen “that we should be holy and blameless,” not because we were. The purpose is the praise of his glorious grace. The result is humility and security: God began the work, and he will finish it (Philippians 1:6; Romans 8:29-30).

Christians have understood the details differently. In the Reformed (Calvinist) tradition, God unconditionally chose particular individuals for salvation before the foundation of the world, and he effectually calls them so that they certainly believe. In the Arminian tradition, God elects on the basis of his foreknowledge of who would respond in faith, or elects the church as a corporate body in Christ and individuals as they join it by faith. Other views stress corporate election: Christ is the Chosen One, and those who are in him share his election. Roman Catholic and Orthodox traditions have their own formulations. These debates have been serious and will not be settled here.

Some guidelines help us read faithfully. Hold the mystery: God is sovereign, and human beings are genuinely responsible. Scripture teaches both, and we are not asked to fully reconcile them. Remember the purpose: Paul teaches election to comfort and to elicit praise, not to discourage evangelism. The same Paul who wrote Romans 9 wrote Romans 10 about the necessity of preaching. And never use election as an excuse for pride or fatalism. The right response is worship.
interpretation:
In Ephesians 1, election is first of all about Christ. We were chosen “in him.” Jesus is the chosen one, and we share in his election by union with him. The purpose of election is holiness and adoption. It is not a doctrine of exclusion but of grace: “In love he predestined us for adoption.” Everything is done “according to the purpose of his will,” “to the praise of his glorious grace.”

Romans 9 focuses on the question of Israel: why have so many of God’s people not believed? Paul’s answer begins with a reminder: “Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.” The promise always went through God’s choice: Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau. “Though they were not yet born and had done nothing either good or bad, in order that God’s purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls.” Paul anticipates the objection: is God unjust? “By no means! For he says to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy.” Salvation “depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy.” No one deserves mercy; if God gives it to some, no one is wronged. The potter has the right over the clay. And Paul adds that God endures with much patience vessels of wrath prepared for destruction, in order to make known the riches of his glory for vessels of mercy, “whom he has prepared beforehand for glory, even us whom he has called, not from the Jews only but also from the Gentiles.”

If you are a Christian, the doctrine means that your salvation does not ultimately rest on your grip on God but on his grip on you. If you are not sure whether you are chosen, the answer is found in the gospel call: come to Christ. “Whoever believes in him will not be put to shame.” No one who comes to him is cast out (John 6:37).
connection: John 6:37-44 and 15:16 speak of the Father giving and drawing. Acts 13:48 says as many as were appointed to eternal life believed. Romans 8:28-30 gives the golden chain. 2 Thessalonians 2:13 speaks of being chosen as firstfruits. 1 Peter 1:1-2 and 2 Peter 1:10 speak of election. Deuteronomy 7:6-8 gives God’s choice of Israel from love. 2 Peter 3:9 and 1 Timothy 2:4 speak of God’s desire that all be saved. Revelation 13:8 and 17:8 mention the book of life. Philippians 2:12-13 pairs God’s work and ours.
application:
Thank God for choosing you, if you are in Christ. Let it humble you and make you secure.

Pray for someone who does not believe. The doctrine of election should drive us to pray and to share the gospel, not away from it.

When you disagree with another Christian on this doctrine, respond with love, remembering that both of you are seeking to honor God’s word.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for choosing you in Christ before the foundation of the world.
Tell him what you cannot fully understand, and rest in him.
Ask him to make you humble and holy.
